title: Justice

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

One pizza, a table of hungry people. 'Make sure this kid gets fed' is a question about one person. Justice asks a different question entirely: how do we cut the pizza so nobody gets cheated? It is the fairness-of-the-slices principle, and its core rule is that a smaller slice needs a reason that actually relates to the situation — not someone's accent, job, or bank balance. Any time you find yourself comparing how two patients were treated, you have moved into justice territory.

### Question 2

Four different fairness jobs. Distributive: who gets how much of the cake. Procedural: were the cutting rules announced ahead of time and applied the same way to everyone. Restorative: someone ruined the cake, how do we repair the damage. Retributive: someone stole the cake, what consequence fits. Ten ventilators and twenty patients is squarely a cake-slicing problem, so it is distributive. Notice that procedural is the one that often rides along with it — how you decide matters even after you have named what you are dividing.

### Question 3

A coach hands out shoes. Two players with the same size feet get the same shoes: treat equals equally. A player with much larger feet gets larger shoes: treat unequals unequally, and it is still fair because foot size is relevant. Give larger shoes to whoever's family donated money and it collapses, because money has nothing to do with feet. That is the whole formal principle — and notice it never tells you which differences count. That blank is exactly what the arguments over need versus benefit versus waiting time are trying to fill.

### Question 4

Three people of different heights watch a game over a fence. Equality hands all three the same box, so the shortest still sees nothing. Equity gives the shortest the tallest box, and now everyone sees the game. The boxes are deliberately unequal, because the goal was never matching boxes — it was an equal chance to watch. Health equity works the same way: the same shot at being healthy, not necessarily the same amount of stuff. So 'we gave everyone the same thing' can be true and still leave a gap untouched.

### Question 5

If a coach posts the selection rules before tryouts and a neutral evaluator does the picking, you may still not make the team — but the rules were the same for everyone and you can point at them and challenge them. If the coach instead decides quietly in the moment, favoritism creeps in even when nobody intends it. Publishing triage criteria is that posted rule. It cannot conjure ventilators; it makes the way we choose defensible, and it keeps your nurse arguing for you rather than rationing against you.

### Question 6

Suppose a company tests a new mattress on people living in a shelter, because they are easy to find and unlikely to object, then sells the mattress to homeowners. Even if the test is safe and everyone signs the forms, the arrangement is lopsided: one group carries the risk, a different group collects the payoff. Belmont's justice question is exactly that — who takes the risk and who gets the reward — and the answer should be roughly the same population. Convenience is not a good enough reason to pick who gets experimented on.

### Question 7

Imagine a rule that the tallest people always lose their seat on the bus. It is measurable and you could apply it to everyone identically — but height has nothing to do with who needs the ride, so it stays unfair no matter how evenly you enforce it. Judging ventilator priority by disability works the same way: it measures something real but irrelevant to whether this treatment gets this person through this illness. In the United States it is also more than unfair — it is a civil rights violation with a specific regulation behind it.

### Question 8

Two people fall off the same bike and get the same scraped knee, but only one gets a bandage — and the thing that predicts who does is which language they speak. Nothing about the injury differs, so the only explanation is something that should not have mattered. That is the fingerprint to look for: two similar patients, different care, and the reason has nothing to do with their bodies. Also worth noticing that nobody had to intend it; patterns like this usually run on autopilot.

### Question 9

Think of law as a fence and ethics as a map. EMTALA is the fence: a hospital with an emergency department that participates in Medicare must screen you and stabilize an emergency condition even if you cannot pay, and crossing that fence brings penalties. Justice is the map — it points a direction that usually runs well past where the fence sits. Clearing the legal minimum is not the same as being fair, and the two are enforced by completely different machinery: courts and regulators on one side, professional judgment and licensure on the other.

### Question 10

In 1962 a Seattle committee decided who received the first dialysis machines partly by weighing who seemed more socially valuable — job, church attendance, being a good parent. Public reaction was harsh once it came out, because a small group was quietly ranking whose life counted more. Modern organ rules deliberately restrict themselves to body facts: how sick you are, how well the organ is likely to work in you, how long you have waited. Being famous or wealthy is a fact about your circumstances, not about your liver.

### Question 11

Free tickets go to whoever loads a website first at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday. The rule is identical for everyone, so it feels scrupulously fair — yet the winners are the people with fast internet and a job that lets them stop and click. The rule did not pick favorites; the world had already picked them, and the rule just handed the outcome over to that head start. This is why 'we treated everyone the same' is a claim about the procedure, not proof about the result. Justice asks you to look at who actually ended up with the vaccine.

### Question 12

A clinician staying late for one patient is kindness aimed at a single person — that is beneficence, and it leaves the system exactly as it was. Changing the clinic's hours, adding a shuttle, and hiring interpreters because an entire neighborhood could not get through the door is a different kind of act: it repairs the door. Justice is about the door, meaning who can reach care at all. And notice the repair was not identical for everyone — that community got extra precisely because it started further behind, which is equity doing its job.
